content: Neonates may require surgical intervention for conditions such as diaphragmatic hernia, gastroschisis, congenital heart disease, hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, or complications of prematurity like necrotizing enterocolitis, spontaneous intestinal perforation, and retinopathy of prematurity. Postoperative pain management in these neonates can involve systemic opioids, non-pharmacological methods, or other pharmacological agents. Commonly used opioids in neonates include morphine, fentanyl, and remifentanil. However, there is concern regarding the potential adverse effects of opioids on the developing brain, making it critical to evaluate their safety and efficacy in this vulnerable population. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and harms of systemic opioid analgesics in neonates undergoing surgery, specifically focusing on outcomes such as all-cause mortality, pain relief, and significant neurodevelopmental disabilities. Comparisons were made between systemic opioids and no intervention, placebo, non-pharmacological interventions, other opioids, or alternative drugs. The search strategy included databases such as Cochrane CENTRAL, MEDLINE via PubMed, and CINAHL, as well as clinical trial registries and conference proceedings. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving preterm and term neonates up to a postmenstrual age of 46 weeks who experienced postoperative pain. The trials compared systemic opioids to placebo, non-pharmacological interventions, other opioids, or alternative drugs. Four RCTs involving 331 neonates from four countries were included. These studies primarily involved neonates undergoing major thoracic or abdominal surgeries, which typically necessitate postoperative opioid administration. Neonates undergoing minor surgeries or those exposed to opioids prior to the trials were excluded. The trials compared opioids to placebo, fentanyl to tramadol, and morphine to paracetamol. However, no meta-analyses could be conducted due to the limited number of outcomes reported in the included studies. The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to imprecision and methodological limitations. In the comparison of opioids versus placebo or no treatment, two trials were included. These trials compared tramadol or tapentadol to placebo. No data were available on critical outcomes such as pain, major neurodevelopmental disability, or long-term cognitive and educational outcomes. The evidence regarding the effect of tramadol on all-cause mortality during initial hospitalization was highly uncertain (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.70; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.05; 71 participants, 1 study). No data were reported on retinopathy of prematurity or intraventricular hemorrhage. No trials were identified that compared opioids to non-pharmacological interventions. In the head-to-head comparison of different opioids, one trial compared fentanyl to tramadol. No data were available on critical outcomes such as pain, major neurodevelopmental disability, or long-term cognitive and educational outcomes. The evidence regarding the effect of fentanyl on all-cause mortality during initial hospitalization was highly uncertain (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.64; RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.13; 171 participants, 1 study). No data were reported on retinopathy of prematurity or intraventricular hemorrhage. In the comparison of opioids to other analgesics, one trial compared morphine to paracetamol. The evidence regarding the effect of morphine on pain, as measured by COMFORT pain scores, was highly uncertain (MD 0.10, 95% CI -0.85 to 1.05; 71 participants, 1 study). No data were available on other critical outcomes, including major neurodevelopmental disability, long-term cognitive and educational outcomes, all-cause mortality during initial hospitalization, retinopathy of prematurity, or intraventricular hemorrhage. In conclusion, there is limited evidence regarding the use of systemic opioids for postoperative pain management in neonates. The available data are insufficient to determine whether tramadol reduces mortality compared to placebo, whether fentanyl reduces mortality compared to tramadol, or whether morphine reduces pain compared to paracetamol. None of the included studies reported on critical outcomes such as pain relief, major neurodevelopmental disability, long-term cognitive and educational outcomes, retinopathy of prematurity, or intraventricular hemorrhage. Additionally, no studies were identified that compared opioids to non-pharmacological interventions. Further high-quality research is needed to address these gaps in evidence.
